cultivar: Wuyi cai cha (local small-leaf population bushes)
processing: Fully oxidised: a bud with two or three leaves is withered indoors or in the sun, rolled, oxidised and dried with hot air or charcoal, with no pine smoke at any stage.
harvest_season: Spring, from late April to late May at Tongmu's altitude, usually picked after the bud teas; one picking a year in the reserve.
appearance_dry: Tight, wiry, slightly curved dark strands with a dull sheen and few tips.
appearance_wet: Small, even copper-red leaves, soft and whole.
taste_profile: Dried longan, honey and sweet potato with a cocoa base and a clean, cool mountain finish; faint pine-forest notes in some lots come from the place, not from smoke.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan, water near the boil, short steeps, no rinse. It is robust: a long steep gets strong but not harsh. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest after a few months' rest, and it is one of the few Chinese blacks that drinks well in its second and third year; Tongmu makers often say it rounds out after a year. Lao cong (old-bush) lots and single-village lots are sold with the year stated.
description:
Zheng Shan Xiao Zhong is the black tea of Tongmu, the village in the Wuyi nature reserve that is usually credited with inventing black tea at all, somewhere around the seventeenth century. The name means 'small-leaf cultivar from the true mountain', 'true mountain' being the reserve itself, and the unsmoked version is what Tongmu makers now mostly produce: the same leaf and process as the famous smoked tea, minus the pine fires.

The leaf is a bud with two or three leaves from the local small-leaf bushes, withered, rolled, oxidised and dried with hot air or charcoal. Unsmoked Xiao Zhong became the norm in the 2000s, after Jin Jun Mei taught the market that Tongmu's leaf had plenty to say without smoke; it is still often made by the same families in the same wooden drying houses, just without lighting the pine.

In the cup it is dried longan and honey over cocoa, with a sweet-potato warmth and a cool, clean finish that people call 'mountain air' for want of a better word. Some lots have a faint pine-forest note anyway, from the place rather than the process. It is sturdy: water near the boil, short steeps, eight or more infusions, and even a forgotten long steep comes out strong rather than bitter.

It is sold by the current spring harvest, usually rested a few months before release, and it ages gracefully for two or three years. Grades follow picking standard (Xiao Chi Gan and Da Chi Gan are the names for finer and coarser pickings) and bush age, with 'lao cong' from old bushes at the top. The caveat is the same as for every Tongmu tea: 'zheng shan' is used far outside the reserve, so buy from sellers who name the village. Real Tongmu tea is never cheap, but it is not Jin Jun Mei money either.

If you only know Lapsang souchong as the smoky tea, this is the version to drink to understand why Tongmu was famous before anyone lit a fire under it.
sources_note: Origin as 'the first black tea' and its dating (late Ming / early Qing, c. 17th century) is the conventional account; stated as such rather than as hard fact.
